messages.subject: Re: R/QTL, QTLBIM, BayesQTLBIC, xQTL, etc
parts:
After looking through more of the literature and the book on R/QTL, it seems like the stepwiseqtl function in R/QTL is the most reliably way to proceed with the analysis of coming up with QTL models for the data and using scantwo with permutations to determine the threshold values for each phenotype.
Finally to assign explained-variance using the fitqtl on the model output from stepwiseqtl.
 

On Wednesday, September 19, 2012 12:28:42 PM UTC+2, Kevin wrote:
I want to perform a simple linkage analysis on a hybrid F2 (outcross to form F1, intercross to form F2) population and I have tried a multitude of tools to examine the data.

The first I used was R/QTL, which requires you as far as I can tell to build the models manually (from scanone, scantwo etc) and then adding and removing loci as needed.

The other tools such as QTLBIM and BayesQTLBIC will generate Multiqtl models more or less automatically. Are these methods now commonly accepted for QTL analysis?

The uniqueness and interest of my data is in the phenotypes we measured rather than trying to find new creative models or statistical techniques.

Do the members of this group have a general suggestion for how the other freely available tools should, if at all, be integrated in the analysis pathway for a 'standard' experiment? It seems at least initially that the amount of overlap between many of the tools is quite large and a number of the features or analysis types in the newer tools are rather 'experimental' still.

Thank you,
Kevin
